strengths: Significance: Generating synthetic outliers in feature space is a useful approach when external OOD training data are unavailable. Combining global PCA boundaries, class-specific LDA boundaries, and Mahalanobis filtering provides a concrete, potentially practical contribution.

Empirical merits: Table 2 reports substantial CIFAR-10 improvements, reducing average FPR@95 from 9.41% for CIDER to 0.12%, while increasing ID accuracy to 97.31%. Table 5 also reports improvements on both semantic and background shifts in text.

Evaluation and presentation: The paper evaluates both ViT and BERT, includes several training and post-processing baselines, and reports ID accuracy alongside multiple detection metrics. Component ablations, hyperparameter studies, computational comparisons, and implementation settings provide useful supporting material.

Limitations and ethics: The authors acknowledge weaker PCA-only performance, difficulty generating inter-class outliers for many classes, and the gap between representational existence and successful training. These are useful acknowledgments. No material research-ethics concern is apparent from the described benchmark experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 5 is not established. Definition 5 applies Lebesgue measure to distributions without defining a measurable parameterization or the meaning of its limits. In Appendix F, an integrated approximation bound is converted into claims about arbitrary finite inputs and hypothesis-class membership without a valid sampling argument. Equations (48)–(49) multiply event-probability bounds without establishing independence. Consequently, the central probability-of-learnability bound and ensuing model-scaling claims are unsupported.

Soundness—Theorem 4 also has substantive proof gaps. In Lemma 1, the construction sets the network bias b2 equal to the negative input-dependent hidden state, which is not a permissible fixed bias. Furthermore, the necessity argument establishes finite VC dimension separately for each fixed architecture, whereas Definition 4 uses the union over architectures; this does not establish the stated result for that union. These issues require corrected constructions and quantifiers.

Theory-to-method connection: Section 3 equates having finite training data with the theorem's assumption that the entire input domain X is finite. These are different conditions. The representational results also do not establish that GROD's synthetic samples or optimization procedure guarantee learnability. The assertion that cross-entropy violates the theorem's label-loss condition, and that the proposed combined loss remedies this, lacks a precise derivation connecting probabilistic predictions to that condition.

Empirical support and scope: The broad SOTA claim is inconsistent with the tables. On CIFAR-100, GROD's average AUROC is 91.34%, below CIDER's 91.57%; on ImageNet-200, its average FPR@95 is 18.26%, versus CIDER's 15.97%, and its average AUROC is below MSP. The striking near-perfect CIFAR-10 result has no reported multi-seed uncertainty, and Table 6 shows an unusually large jump only with all components enabled. Repeated runs and ablations separating PCA/LDA generation from the logit adjustment and VIM post-processing are needed to establish robustness and attribution.

Reproducibility: Important implementation choices remain ambiguous. Equation (3) invokes inverses of dimensionality-reducing PCA/LDA maps without specifying a reconstruction or original-sample retrieval rule. The filtering parameter lambda is called learnable, but its update through a hard selection mask is unspecified. Equation (14) tests for class K+1 after describing removal of that coordinate. Algorithm 1 places training updates inside the condition for excess synthetic samples. The abstract's code-availability statement supplies no usable link.

Dataset specification: Section 4.2 describes CLINC150 as having ten categories without documenting a subset or relabeling, which affects both comparability and the class-dependent generation rule. The assertion that image ID/OOD categories are disjoint also needs an explicit class-overlap audit for the ImageNet-derived datasets and CIFAR pairings. ImageNet-1K pretraining exposure should be distinguished clearly from the absence of OOD exposure during fine-tuning.

Originality and presentation: The distinctive methodological contribution is the particular projection-and-filtering construction; synthetic feature outliers, auxiliary OOD objectives, and transformer approximation results already have substantial precedent, including cited NPOS and Fang et al. The manuscript needs a sharper account of the new understanding beyond combining these elements. Undefined or inconsistent notation and broken references further impede verification. Overall, the practical idea has merit, but central theoretical errors and unresolved experimental reproducibility issues prevent acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Generating synthetic OOD features without an external outlier dataset addresses a useful practical problem. Combining global PCA boundaries, class-sensitive LDA boundaries, and distance filtering offers a plausible approach.

Empirical merits: Table 2 reports substantial CIFAR-10 improvements, reducing average FPR@95 from 9.41% for CIDER to 0.12%, while improving ID accuracy. Table 5 also reports improvements on both text OOD tasks. Evaluation across vision and language, computational comparisons, and component ablations are valuable.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the appendices provide proofs, pseudocode, training hyperparameters, hardware details, and checkpoint-selection criteria. The discussion acknowledges weaker performance without LDA and difficulties generating inter-class outliers for many-class tasks.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 4 has a concrete proof defect. In Appendix E, Lemma 1 sets the network bias b2 = −h(i−3) to cancel the residual connection. This hidden representation depends on the input, whereas a network bias must be fixed across inputs. Consequently, the stated network inclusion is not established by this construction. Furthermore, the necessity argument concerns each fixed architecture, whereas Definition 4 uses a union over architectures; the quantifiers need reconciliation.

Soundness—Theorem 5 lacks a well-defined probabilistic foundation. Definition 5 applies Lebesgue measure to distributions and uses limits without specifying a probability space or limiting procedure. Lemma 5, Equations 48–49, multiplies marginal success bounds across coordinates and hypotheses without establishing independence. An approximation bound holding for most inputs also does not establish exact representability on every point of a fixed finite domain. These gaps undermine the claimed probability-of-learnability bound.

Theory-to-method connection: The manuscript treats finiteness of the input domain |X| as if it followed from having a finite training dataset. These are different assumptions. The theorems concern existence or learnability within hypothesis classes, not convergence of GROD training or coverage of real OOD distributions by its synthetic features. The proposed softmax loss is also not formally connected to the discrete label-loss condition in the theorems. Thus, claims that GROD guarantees learnability and that adding the binary loss ensures the theoretical conditions are unsupported.

Significance and claim calibration: The results do not support the blanket state-of-the-art claim. In Table 3, GROD's average AUROC is 91.34%, below CIDER's 91.57%; on Tiny ImageNet its FPR@95 is 38.84%, versus 30.22% for VIM. In Table 4, average FPR@95 is 18.26%, versus 15.97% for CIDER, and average AUROC is below MSP. The useful empirical contribution appears more conditional than the abstract and conclusion suggest.

Experimental reliability: The near-perfect CIFAR-10 result and abrupt improvement when all components are combined warrant repeated runs and uncertainty estimates, which are absent from the main benchmark tables. The paper does not isolate the contribution of the inference-time logit adjustment from feature generation and VIM. Hyperparameters are motivated using OOD performance curves, but an independent tuning protocol is not specified. These omissions limit confidence in the magnitude and robustness of the gains without implying misconduct.

Reproducibility and presentation: Section 4.2 describes CLINC150 as having ten categories, without explaining a subset or label regrouping. This matters directly because K controls whether LDA is enabled. Equation 3 invokes inverse mappings of dimension-reducing projections without specifying reconstruction or selection of original samples. The filtering parameter λ is called learnable, but its update through hard filtering is unexplained; Algorithm 1 instead calls α learnable despite Appendix J giving fixed values. The abstract's code-availability statement is unfinished and supplies no link. These ambiguities impede faithful reproduction.

Originality, limitations, and ethics: The potentially original contribution is the particular synthesis-and-filtering combination; its distinction from existing virtual-outlier methods is insufficiently established beyond the NPOS comparison. The theoretical contribution largely adapts prior learnability and approximation results, with the unresolved gaps above. The acknowledged limitations are appropriate, but the paper should additionally delimit its guarantees and discuss semantic overlap and ImageNet-1K pretraining exposure when interpreting OOD benchmarks. I identify no material ethical violation; the decisive reasons for rejection are technical soundness and insufficiently supported central claims.

strengths: Significance: Improving OOD detection without external outlier data is useful. GROD offers a practical combination of feature-space boundary sampling, PCA/LDA projections, Mahalanobis filtering, and joint classification losses.

Empirical merits: Table 2 reports striking CIFAR-10 improvements, reducing average FPR@95 from 9.41% for CIDER to 0.12%, while improving ID accuracy. Table 5 also reports improvements on both text OOD tasks. Evaluation across vision and language is a strength.

Presentation and reproducibility: The overall pipeline is understandable, and the manuscript provides component ablations, hyperparameter studies, pseudocode, training settings, and extensive theoretical appendices. It acknowledges weaker performance without LDA and difficulties generating inter-class outliers for many-class tasks.
weaknesses: Soundness—central proofs contain substantive gaps. In Appendix E, Lemma 1 sets the network bias b2 = −h(i−3), which depends on the input; this does not construct a network with fixed parameters. In Appendix F, Eqs. 48–49 multiply probability bounds across coordinates and hypotheses without establishing independence. These steps do not establish the claimed guarantees.

Soundness—Theorem 5 lacks a well-defined probabilistic foundation. Definition 5 applies Lebesgue measure to distributions and introduces limits without specifying a limiting process or probability law over domains. Moreover, an integrated approximation bound over continuous inputs does not ensure correctness on an arbitrary finite support. The subsequent probability of representing every labeling, and hence the learnability bound, is unsupported.

The theoretical connection to GROD is overstated. The finite input-space assumption |X| < infinity is conflated with having a finite training dataset on page 6. Existence of a suitable hypothesis or learning algorithm does not guarantee that the proposed loss, synthetic outliers, and optimization recover it. The label-pair loss assumption is also not rigorously connected to the probability-based cross-entropy objective. No result establishes coverage of real OOD distributions by GROD's synthetic features.

Reproducibility has material gaps. Eq. 3 invokes inverses of dimension-reducing PCA/LDA mappings without specifying a reconstruction or preimage-selection rule. The filtering parameter lambda is called learnable, but its update through hard selection is unspecified. Algorithm 1 places model updates inside the condition that excess outliers require subsampling, apparently skipping other batches. CLINC150 is described as having ten classes without explaining the reduction from 150 intents. These ambiguities affect the implemented method and benchmark interpretation.

The evaluation does not substantiate the broad SOTA claim. In Table 3, GROD's average AUROC is below CIDER's (91.34% versus 91.57%); in Table 4, its average FPR@95 is worse than CIDER's (18.26% versus 15.97%) and AUROC is below MSP's (95.24% versus 95.18%). The real-data results lack uncertainty estimates. Given the unusually large CIFAR-10 gain, repeated runs and an ablation isolating the logit adjustment and ViM post-processing are particularly important.

Originality and scope: The distinctive contribution is the particular projection-based synthesis and filtering strategy, while synthetic outlier training, binary OOD objectives, and ViM build on established approaches. Stronger controlled comparisons with alternative synthesis strategies are needed to isolate this contribution. Detection results also do not establish the broader claims about prediction or generalization on unknown distributions. No material research-ethics concern is apparent; the rejection is driven by technical and evidential weaknesses.

strengths: Significance: Reliable OOD detection is an important problem, and GROD offers a potentially useful approach that synthesizes feature-space outliers without requiring an external outlier dataset. The evaluation spans vision and text with four transformer backbones.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports substantial improvements on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. For CIFAR-10, average FPR@95 decreases from CIDER's 9.41% to 0.12%, while ID accuracy improves. Table 8 includes useful comparisons against Gaussian and uniform outliers, and the appendix examines projection methods, filtering, soft labels, and hyperparameters.

Originality: Combining global PCA boundaries, class-specific LDA boundaries, Mahalanobis filtering, and soft outlier labels is a plausible methodological contribution. Connecting transformer approximation theory with OOD learnability is also a worthwhile research direction, although the proposed theoretical connection is not established soundly.

Presentation and limitations: The overall algorithmic workflow is understandable, and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail, including covariance regularization and ID-validation-based checkpoint selection. The manuscript acknowledges optimization gaps, architectural limitations, and exposure to some OOD categories during pretraining. No specific material research-ethics concern is evident.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorems 4.5–4.6 lack a well-defined probability foundation. Definition 4.4 applies Lebesgue measure in R^d to distributions or collections of distributions without defining a corresponding measurable space or sampling law; interpreting these objects as finite supports instead gives zero Lebesgue measure. Appendix C then turns an integrated approximation bound into probabilities of exact hypothesis-class membership. An error bound for a random input does not establish representability on every point of a fixed finite domain. Equations (41)–(42) additionally multiply success probabilities without establishing independence. These issues invalidate the claimed learnability-probability and scaling guarantees as presented.

Soundness—Theorem 4.3 has unresolved proof gaps. Appendix B proves necessity only for each fixed finite architecture H^(l,m), whereas the theorem concerns H, defined as the union over architectures; finite VC dimension of each component does not establish the required property of that union. Moreover, the FCNN embedding proof sets the bias b2 = -h_(i-3), which depends on the input and therefore is not a valid fixed network parameter. Lemma 4.2 also claims arbitrary-accuracy universal approximation with both depth and width fixed independently of the target and accuracy, requiring substantial justification; for a single token, the specified architecture reduces to a fixed-size piecewise-linear network.

Soundness—the theory does not guarantee GROD. The label-based loss condition l(y2,y1) ≤ l(K+1,y1) is treated as a requirement on the training cross-entropy surrogate, but this identification is not proved. Adding the binary loss does not by itself establish the ordering for arbitrary predictive distributions. More fundamentally, existence of a PAC learner or an expressive hypothesis class does not imply that GROD's synthetic outliers and gradient-based training produce that learner. Claims that GROD 'ensures learnability' and converges to the target mapping exceed the results.

Empirical significance is overstated. Performance is not consistently state of the art across the reported metrics: CIDER has lower ImageNet-200 FPR@95 than GROD (15.97% versus 17.16%), and Table 3 shows several Llama semantic-shift AUROCs above GROD's 93.64%. GROD's Llama background-shift FPR@95 remains 83.28%. Main benchmark tables provide no uncertainty estimates or clear repeat counts, making smaller gains difficult to assess. The ablations also do not clearly isolate the modified ViM/logit-adjustment contribution from the proposed training method.

Reproducibility remains inadequate for the unusually large reported improvements. Appendix E ends with 'The code is publicly available at' but supplies no URL. Equations (16)/(64) call unnormalized exponential weights soft labels without specifying normalization and mix class indices i and j in the distance terms. Equation (68) first retains only K logits but subsequently tests whether their argmax is K+1. The update mechanism for the learnable hard-filter parameter λ and Llama LoRA configuration are also insufficiently specified.

Presentation and originality of the theoretical contribution need clarification. The manuscript conflates finite input-domain cardinality with training-sample count and approximation capacity with statistical learnability. The qualitative condition closely follows Fang et al., while the approximation machinery is imported from existing transformer theory. A valid extension could still provide useful new understanding, but the central new quantitative claims currently lack sound support. The promising empirical method does not compensate for these foundational deficiencies.

strengths: Significance: Understanding when transformers can detect OOD inputs is a useful research objective. GROD also addresses a practical setting by synthesizing auxiliary outliers from ID features without requiring real OOD training examples.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports substantial improvements on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. For CIFAR-10, average FPR@95 decreases from CIDER’s 9.41% to 0.12%, while ID accuracy improves. Evaluation spans image and text tasks and four transformer backbones.

Originality: Combining global PCA boundaries, class-dependent LDA boundaries, Mahalanobis filtering, and soft labels offers a potentially useful synthesis strategy. Table 8 and Figure 6 investigate several components, including comparisons with Gaussian and uniform outlier generation.

Presentation and reproducibility: The manuscript supplies extensive appendices with proofs, algorithm details, hyperparameters, dataset descriptions, and component ablations. Appendix F specifies checkpoint selection using ID validation accuracy. The discussion acknowledges distributional and architectural limitations; I identify no material research-ethics concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—invalid expressivity construction: Lemma B.1, supporting Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.3, cancels a residual connection by setting the bias b2 = -h_{i-3}. However, h_{i-3} depends on the input, whereas b2 must be a fixed model parameter. This does not construct a single transformer implementing the claimed FCNN over all inputs. A valid construction, with the stated depth and width, is needed.

Soundness—hypothesis-space mismatch: Definitions 3.2–3.4 define H as a union over arbitrarily large finite architectures. The necessity proof of Theorem 4.3 instead establishes finite VC dimension and invokes impossibility separately for each fixed H^(l,m). This does not establish the claimed result for their union. Remark B.5 recognizes the capacity issue without resolving the quantifier mismatch. The same distinction affects the finite-dimension argument in Section 4.2.

Soundness—the central probability bounds are not established: Definition 4.4 applies Lebesgue measure in R^d to distributions or collections of distributions without defining a suitable probability space or the limiting operation. If interpreted as finite supports, those supports have zero Lebesgue measure. Moreover, Appendix C moves from approximation-error probabilities over inputs to probabilities that entire functions belong to a deterministic hypothesis class. Equations (41)–(42) multiply success probabilities without establishing independence. Consequently, Theorems 4.5–4.6 do not provide justified learnability probabilities or capacity scaling laws as written.

Soundness—theory does not guarantee GROD: The loss condition l(y2,y1) <= l(K+1,y1) concerns a loss on discrete prediction/label pairs; it is not shown to hold for the proposed probability-dependent cross-entropy objective. More fundamentally, existence or learnability results do not establish convergence of GROD’s optimization or show that its synthetic feature distribution represents unknown real OOD inputs. Claims that GROD 'ensures learnability' and converges to the target mapping with sufficient depth exceed the analysis. The acknowledged theory–practice gap is appropriate, but it does not support these guarantees.

Evaluation and significance: The blanket claim of consistently achieving state-of-the-art performance is contradicted by the reported results. In Table 3, GROD’s CLINC150 AUROC is 93.64 versus ASH’s 93.69, and its ID accuracy is below several alternatives. On IMDB, ID accuracy is 71.15 versus CIDER’s 76.26, while GROD’s FPR@95 remains 83.28%. Table 1 also gives CIDER a better ImageNet-200 FPR@95. The main benchmark tables lack uncertainty estimates, and no experiment directly validates the proposed capacity-dependent bounds.

Reproducibility and presentation: Appendix E ends with 'The code is publicly available at' but provides no link. Several implementation details remain ambiguous: Equation (64) supplies unnormalized soft-label weights with inconsistent class indices, and Equation (68) discards the OOD coordinate before referring to its argmax. The manuscript should specify the exact label normalization and modified ViM computation and isolate the contribution of that inference modification. These details matter particularly given the unusually large CIFAR-10 improvement.

Originality and overall assessment: The theoretical contribution primarily transfers prior OOD learnability and transformer approximation results, while GROD combines established synthesis and scoring ingredients. Such a contribution could still be valuable with valid new understanding and convincing validation. Here, however, the unresolved proof errors affect the paper’s central claims, and promising empirical results do not compensate for them. Substantial theoretical repair and clearer reproducibility are required before acceptance.

strengths: Significance: Improving transformer OOD detection without requiring real auxiliary outliers is a useful goal. GROD offers a concrete approach combining PCA/LDA boundary selection, synthetic feature generation, Mahalanobis filtering, and an additional binary loss.

Empirical merits: The reported image results are promising. Table 1 improves average FPR@95 from 9.41 to 0.12 on CIFAR-10 and from 35.97 to 22.30 on CIFAR-100 relative to CIDER, while improving ID accuracy. Evaluation across ViT, BERT, GPT-2, and Llama provides useful breadth.

Originality: The combination of global and class-specific synthetic outliers with filtering and soft labels provides a potentially useful methodological contribution. Table 8 and Figures 5–6 investigate components, generation strategies, and hyperparameters rather than reporting only aggregate performance.

Presentation and transparency: The algorithm overview is understandable, and the appendices provide substantial implementation and experimental detail. The paper acknowledges the distinction between representational existence and practical optimization, as well as pretraining exposure to some OOD categories. I see no material research-ethics concern in the described experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness—Theorem 4.3 is not established by the supplied proof. In Lemma B.1, the construction sets b2 = −h(i−3), but this hidden representation depends on the input, whereas a network bias must be fixed. Thus the stated FCNN embedding does not follow. Additionally, the necessity argument establishes finite VC dimension for each fixed H(l,m), while the theorem concerns H, the union over arbitrary depths and budgets. The fixed-class argument does not automatically establish the union-class result.

Soundness—The probability underlying Theorems 4.5–4.6 is not adequately defined. Definition 4.4 applies Lebesgue measure in R^d to distributions or collections of distributions without specifying a corresponding measurable space or sampling law; interpreting these objects as finite supports instead gives zero Lebesgue measure. Consequently, the claimed 'probability of learnability' lacks a clear mathematical interpretation.

Soundness—Appendix C does not justify converting an integrated approximation bound into exact hypothesis-class containment. An average error bound under Lebesgue measure does not control arbitrary finite support points, which can all lie in an exceptional set. Equations (41)–(42) also multiply marginal success bounds across coordinates and hypotheses without establishing independence. These issues directly undermine the central capacity-dependent learnability bounds.

Theory–algorithm connection: Even repaired expressivity results would not establish that GROD learns reliably from its synthetic outliers. The theorems do not analyze GROD's generation procedure, optimization, or transfer from synthetic to real OOD distributions. Moreover, the condition on discrete paired losses is not shown to follow from the proposed probabilistic cross-entropy objective. Claims that GROD 'ensures learnability' or gains a theoretical guarantee therefore exceed the analysis.

Empirical claims and significance: Performance is not consistently superior across the reported settings. CIDER has better ImageNet-200 average FPR@95 than GROD (15.97 versus 17.16); GEN-L outperforms GROD on GPT-2 background-shift FPR@95 and AUROC (Table 7); and Llama results do not consistently improve ID accuracy or semantic-shift AUROC. The main benchmark tables lack uncertainty estimates, and the modified VIM/logit adjustment is not separately ablated, limiting attribution of the gains.

Reproducibility and presentation: The statement 'The code is publicly available at' has no accompanying URL. Equation (64) does not specify normalization of its soft-label weights; Equation (68) checks for class K+1 after the preceding text says only the first K outputs are retained. Appendix G also describes CLINC150 as having ten categories without explaining the subset. These ambiguities materially affect replication. Despite useful limitations discussions, the manuscript needs clearer separation of proven results, empirical observations, and conjectures. The promising practical contribution does not outweigh the unresolved flaws in its central theoretical claims.
